definition: A mutex (mutual exclusion object) is a program object that allows multiple program threads to share the same resource, such as file access, but not simultaneously.
details: A mutex (mutual exclusion object) is a program object that allows multiple program threads to share the same resource, such as file access, but not simultaneously. When a program is locked by a mutex, no other thread can access the locked region of code until the mutex is unlocked.

explainer.lead: A mutex (mutual exclusion object) lets multiple program threads share a resource such as file access, but not simultaneously. It matters because it prevents concurrent code from corrupting shared state.

tiers.eli5: Like a single key to a shared bathroom: whoever holds the key goes in, and everyone else waits outside.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers lock a mutex around a critical section and unlock it when done, ensuring only one thread enters. A pitfall is holding a lock too long or acquiring locks in inconsistent order, causing contention or deadlock.
tiers.paperLevel: A lock object with acquire and release operations guaranteeing mutual exclusion over a critical region. Nothing else may access the locked region until the mutex is unlocked.

explainer.example: Two threads incrementing a shared counter each acquire the mutex first, so no increment is lost.
